Context: P-glycoprotein (Pgp, also called MDR1 or ABCB1) is an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) efflux transporter expressed at the apical membrane of intestinal enterocytes, the blood-brain barrier endothelium, renal proximal tubules, and hepatic canalicular membranes. It actively pumps substrates from the intracellular space back into the lumen/blood, reducing oral absorption, brain penetration, and increasing renal and biliary clearance. Inhibition of Pgp can dramatically alter a co-administered drug's pharmacokinetics and tissue distribution. This dataset predicts whether a compound inhibits Pgp.

Pgp has a large, flexible drug-binding pocket within the transmembrane domain that can accommodate structurally diverse substrates and inhibitors. The binding cavity is predominantly hydrophobic, lined by aromatic and aliphatic residues from transmembrane helices TM6 and TM12. It can adopt multiple conformations to accommodate different molecular shapes — this explains Pgp's unusually broad substrate specificity.

Molecular features associated with Pgp inhibition: high lipophilicity (logP > 3) is strongly associated with Pgp inhibition, as hydrophobic molecules partition into the membrane and access the transmembrane binding site. Molecular weight > 400 Da — larger molecules are more likely to inhibit Pgp. Multiple aromatic rings (≥2) provide hydrophobic surface area and van der Waals contacts with the binding cavity. The presence of hydrogen bond acceptors (particularly tertiary amines, ethers, esters) facilitates interactions with polar residues at the edges of the binding pocket. Tertiary or secondary amines (often basic) are common in Pgp inhibitors.

Features associated with non-inhibitors: low lipophilicity (logP < 2) — highly polar, hydrophilic molecules do not partition into the membrane to reach the binding site. Small molecular weight (< 300 Da) — compact molecules tend not to fill the large binding cavity effectively. Few aromatic rings (0-1). High TPSA (> 120 Å²) and many hydrogen bond donors make molecules too polar for membrane partitioning. Fully charged species (strong acids, quaternary ammonium) at physiological pH are generally poor Pgp inhibitors.

Molecular features favoring BBB penetration: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) provides the driving force for passive diffusion across the endothelial lipid bilayer. Being a substrate of nutrient transporters (LAT1 for amino acid-like drugs, GLUT1 for glucose-like structures) can facilitate active uptake.

Features associated with poor BBB penetration: high TPSA (> 90 Å²) strongly predicts exclusion from the CNS. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 3) — each additional donor roughly halves BBB permeability. Compounds that are P-glycoprotein substrates are actively effluxed from the brain — basic amines with MW > 400 and moderate lipophilicity are common Pgp substrates. Charged molecules at pH 7.4 (carboxylates, sulfonates, phosphates, quaternary amines) have very poor passive BBB penetration. High molecular weight (> 500 Da). Context: The Parallel Artificial Membrane Permeability Assay (PAMPA) measures passive transcellular permeability by quantifying how much compound diffuses across an artificial lipid membrane (typically a phospholipid mixture on a filter support) from a donor to an acceptor compartment. Unlike Caco-2 cell assays, PAMPA has no active transporters, no efflux pumps, and no paracellular pathway — it isolates pure passive diffusion. The NCATS variant uses a standardized protocol across a large compound library.

The rate of passive diffusion is governed by the drug's ability to partition from aqueous solution into the lipid bilayer, diffuse across it, and re-partition into the aqueous phase on the other side. This is primarily determined by the molecule's desolvation cost — how much energy is required to strip away the hydration shell of polar groups before entering the hydrophobic membrane interior.

Molecular features favoring high PAMPA permeability: low polar surface area (TPSA < 80 Å² for high permeability, 80-120 Å² for moderate) is the single most predictive descriptor. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 2-3) — each donor adds roughly 10 Å² of TPSA and a strong water interaction that must be broken. Moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) provides the driving force for membrane partitioning. Molecular weight < 500 Da. Intramolecular hydrogen bonds can "mask" polar groups and improve permeability beyond what TPSA alone would predict — this is exploited in cyclic peptide drug design. Compact, low-flexibility conformations reduce the entropic cost of membrane insertion.

Features associated with poor PAMPA permeability: high TPSA (>120 Å²) is the dominant negative predictor. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 4) strongly reduce permeability. Charged species at the assay pH (typically pH 7.4) — carboxylates, phosphates, quaternary amines — have very poor passive diffusion because the charge cannot be buried in the lipid interior. Very hydrophilic molecules (logP < 0) lack the driving force for membrane partitioning. High molecular weight (>600 Da) and many rotatable bonds (>10) also reduce permeability.

Unlike Caco-2 cell assays, PAMPA has no active transporters, no efflux pumps, and no paracellular pathway — it isolates pure passive diffusion. The NCATS variant uses a standardized protocol across a large compound library.

The rate of passive diffusion is governed by the drug's ability to partition from aqueous solution into the lipid bilayer, diffuse across it, and re-partition into the aqueous phase on the other side. This is primarily determined by the molecule's desolvation cost — how much energy is required to strip away the hydration shell of polar groups before entering the hydrophobic membrane interior.

Molecular features favoring high PAMPA permeability: low polar surface area (TPSA < 80 Å² for high permeability, 80-120 Å² for moderate) is the single most predictive descriptor. Moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) provides the driving force for membrane partitioning. Molecular weight < 500 Da. Intramolecular hydrogen bonds can "mask" polar groups and improve permeability beyond what TPSA alone would predict — this is exploited in cyclic peptide drug design. Compact, low-flexibility conformations reduce the entropic cost of membrane insertion.

Features associated with poor PAMPA permeability: high TPSA (>120 Å²) is the dominant negative predictor. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 4) strongly reduce permeability. Charged species at the assay pH (typically pH 7.4) — carboxylates, phosphates, quaternary amines — have very poor passive diffusion because the charge cannot be buried in the lipid interior. Context: The Parallel Artificial Membrane Permeability Assay (PAMPA) measures passive transcellular permeability by quantifying how much compound diffuses across an artificial lipid membrane (typically a phospholipid mixture on a filter support) from a donor to an acceptor compartment. Unlike Caco-2 cell assays, PAMPA has no active transporters, no efflux pumps, and no paracellular pathway — it isolates pure passive diffusion. The NCATS variant uses a standardized protocol across a large compound library.

The rate of passive diffusion is governed by the drug's ability to partition from aqueous solution into the lipid bilayer, diffuse across it, and re-partition into the aqueous phase on the other side. This is primarily determined by the molecule's desolvation cost — how much energy is required to strip away the hydration shell of polar groups before entering the hydrophobic membrane interior.

Molecular features favoring high PAMPA permeability: low polar surface area (TPSA < 80 Å² for high permeability, 80-120 Å² for moderate) is the single most predictive descriptor. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 2-3) — each donor adds roughly 10 Å² of TPSA and a strong water interaction that must be broken. Moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) provides the driving force for membrane partitioning. Molecular weight < 500 Da. Intramolecular hydrogen bonds can "mask" polar groups and improve permeability beyond what TPSA alone would predict — this is exploited in cyclic peptide drug design. Compact, low-flexibility conformations reduce the entropic cost of membrane insertion.

Features associated with poor PAMPA permeability: high TPSA (>120 Å²) is the dominant negative predictor. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 4) strongly reduce permeability. Charged species at the assay pH (typically pH 7.4) — carboxylates, phosphates, quaternary amines — have very poor passive diffusion because the charge cannot be buried in the lipid interior. Very hydrophilic molecules (logP < 0) lack the driving force for membrane partitioning. High molecular weight (>600 Da) and many rotatable bonds (>10) also reduce permeability.

The rate of passive diffusion is governed by the drug's ability to partition from aqueous solution into the lipid bilayer, diffuse across it, and re-partition into the aqueous phase on the other side. This is primarily determined by the molecule's desolvation cost — how much energy is required to strip away the hydration shell of polar groups before entering the hydrophobic membrane interior.

The rate of passive diffusion is governed by the drug's ability to partition from aqueous solution into the lipid bilayer, diffuse across it, and re-partition into the aqueous phase on the other side. This is primarily determined by the molecule's desolvation cost — how much energy is required to strip away the hydration shell of polar groups before entering the hydrophobic membrane interior.

Charged species at the assay pH (typically pH 7.4) — carboxylates, phosphates, quaternary amines — have very poor passive diffusion because the charge cannot be buried in the lipid interior. Unlike Caco-2 cell assays, PAMPA has no active transporters, no efflux pumps, and no paracellular pathway — it isolates pure passive diffusion. The NCATS variant uses a standardized protocol across a large compound library.

The rate of passive diffusion is governed by the drug's ability to partition from aqueous solution into the lipid bilayer, diffuse across it, and re-partition into the aqueous phase on the other side. This is primarily determined by the molecule's desolvation cost — how much energy is required to strip away the hydration shell of polar groups before entering the hydrophobic membrane interior.

Molecular features favoring high PAMPA permeability: low polar surface area (TPSA < 80 Å² for high permeability, 80-120 Å² for moderate) is the single most predictive descriptor. Compact, low-flexibility conformations reduce the entropic cost of membrane insertion.

Charged species at the assay pH (typically pH 7.4) — carboxylates, phosphates, quaternary amines — have very poor passive diffusion because the charge cannot be buried in the lipid interior. Mutagenicity in the Ames test arises through several distinct mechanisms. Unlike Caco-2 cell assays, PAMPA has no active transporters, no efflux pumps, and no paracellular pathway — it isolates pure passive diffusion. The NCATS variant uses a standardized protocol across a large compound library.

The rate of passive diffusion is governed by the drug's ability to partition from aqueous solution into the lipid bilayer, diffuse across it, and re-partition into the aqueous phase on the other side. This is primarily determined by the molecule's desolvation cost — how much energy is required to strip away the hydration shell of polar groups before entering the hydrophobic membrane interior.

Molecular features favoring high PAMPA permeability: low polar surface area (TPSA < 80 Å² for high permeability, 80-120 Å² for moderate) is the single most predictive descriptor. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 2-3) — each donor adds roughly 10 Å² of TPSA and a strong water interaction that must be broken. Moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) provides the driving force for membrane partitioning. Molecular weight < 500 Da. Intramolecular hydrogen bonds can "mask" polar groups and improve permeability beyond what TPSA alone would predict — this is exploited in cyclic peptide drug design. Compact, low-flexibility conformations reduce the entropic cost of membrane insertion.

Charged species at the assay pH (typically pH 7.4) — carboxylates, phosphates, quaternary amines — have very poor passive diffusion because the charge cannot be buried in the lipid interior. Very hydrophilic molecules (logP < 0) lack the driving force for membrane partitioning. High molecular weight (>600 Da) and many rotatable bonds (>10) also reduce permeability.

Context: The Ames test is a bacterial reverse mutation assay that detects compounds capable of inducing genetic damage. Histidine-dependent Salmonella typhimurium (and sometimes E. coli tryptophan auxotrophs) are exposed to the test compound; mutagenic compounds cause reversion mutations that restore the bacteria's ability to synthesize the required amino acid, producing visible colonies. The test is run both with and without metabolic activation (rat liver S9 fraction) to detect pro-mutagens that require CYP-mediated bioactivation.

Mutagenicity in the Ames test arises through several distinct mechanisms. Direct-acting mutagens are electrophilic species that react covalently with DNA bases — alkylating agents (epoxides, aziridines, nitrogen mustards, alkyl halides), Michael acceptors (α,β-unsaturated carbonyls, acrylates, vinyl sulfones), and acylating agents. Pro-mutagens require metabolic activation: aromatic amines are N-hydroxylated by CYP1A2 to form reactive hydroxylamines/nitrenium ions that form DNA adducts; polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are epoxidized by CYP1A1/1B1 to form diol-epoxides; nitroaromatics are reduced to reactive nitroso and hydroxylamine intermediates. The rate of passive diffusion is governed by the drug's ability to partition from aqueous solution into the lipid bilayer, diffuse across it, and re-partition into the aqueous phase on the other side. This is primarily determined by the molecule's desolvation cost — how much energy is required to strip away the hydration shell of polar groups before entering the hydrophobic membrane interior.

Molecular features favoring high PAMPA permeability: low polar surface area (TPSA < 80 Å² for high permeability, 80-120 Å² for moderate) is the single most predictive descriptor. Mutagenicity in the Ames test arises through several distinct mechanisms. Direct-acting mutagens are electrophilic species that react covalently with DNA bases — alkylating agents (epoxides, aziridines, nitrogen mustards, alkyl halides), Michael acceptors (α,β-unsaturated carbonyls, acrylates, vinyl sulfones), and acylating agents. The rate of passive diffusion is governed by the drug's ability to partition from aqueous solution into the lipid bilayer, diffuse across it, and re-partition into the aqueous phase on the other side. Charged species at the assay pH (typically pH 7.4) — carboxylates, phosphates, quaternary amines — have very poor passive diffusion because the charge cannot be buried in the lipid interior. Context: The Parallel Artificial Membrane Permeability Assay (PAMPA) measures passive transcellular permeability by quantifying how much compound diffuses across an artificial lipid membrane (typically a phospholipid mixture on a filter support) from a donor to an acceptor compartment. Unlike Caco-2 cell assays, PAMPA has no active transporters, no efflux pumps, and no paracellular pathway — it isolates pure passive diffusion. The NCATS variant uses a standardized protocol across a large compound library.

The rate of passive diffusion is governed by the drug's ability to partition from aqueous solution into the lipid bilayer, diffuse across it, and re-partition into the aqueous phase on the other side. This is primarily determined by the molecule's desolvation cost — how much energy is required to strip away the hydration shell of polar groups before entering the hydrophobic membrane interior.

Molecular features favoring high PAMPA permeability: low polar surface area (TPSA < 80 Å² for high permeability, 80-120 Å² for moderate) is the single most predictive descriptor. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 2-3) — each donor adds roughly 10 Å² of TPSA and a strong water interaction that must be broken. Moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) provides the driving force for membrane partitioning. Molecular weight < 500 Da. Intramolecular hydrogen bonds can "mask" polar groups and improve permeability beyond what TPSA alone would predict — this is exploited in cyclic peptide drug design. Compact, low-flexibility conformations reduce the entropic cost of membrane insertion.

Features associated with poor PAMPA permeability: high TPSA (>120 Å²) is the dominant negative predictor. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 4) strongly reduce permeability. Charged species at the assay pH (typically pH 7.4) — carboxylates, phosphates, quaternary amines — have very poor passive diffusion because the charge cannot be buried in the lipid interior. Very hydrophilic molecules (logP < 0) lack the driving force for membrane partitioning. High molecular weight (>600 Da) and many rotatable bonds (>10) also reduce permeability.

The test is run both with and without metabolic activation (rat liver S9 fraction) to detect pro-mutagens that require CYP-mediated bioactivation.

Mutagenicity in the Ames test arises through several distinct mechanisms. Direct-acting mutagens are electrophilic species that react covalently with DNA bases — alkylating agents (epoxides, aziridines, nitrogen mustards, alkyl halides), Michael acceptors (α,β-unsaturated carbonyls, acrylates, vinyl sulfones), and acylating agents. Pro-mutagens require metabolic activation: aromatic amines are N-hydroxylated by CYP1A2 to form reactive hydroxylamines/nitrenium ions that form DNA adducts; polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are epoxidized by CYP1A1/1B1 to form diol-epoxides; nitroaromatics are reduced to reactive nitroso and hydroxylamine intermediates. DNA intercalators — large planar polycyclic molecules — can cause frameshift mutations by inserting between base pairs and disrupting replication fidelity.

The test is run both with and without metabolic activation (rat liver S9 fraction) to detect pro-mutagens that require CYP-mediated bioactivation.

Mutagenicity in the Ames test arises through several distinct mechanisms. Direct-acting mutagens are electrophilic species that react covalently with DNA bases — alkylating agents (epoxides, aziridines, nitrogen mustards, alkyl halides), Michael acceptors (α,β-unsaturated carbonyls, acrylates, vinyl sulfones), and acylating agents. Unlike Caco-2 cell assays, PAMPA has no active transporters, no efflux pumps, and no paracellular pathway — it isolates pure passive diffusion. The NCATS variant uses a standardized protocol across a large compound library.

The rate of passive diffusion is governed by the drug's ability to partition from aqueous solution into the lipid bilayer, diffuse across it, and re-partition into the aqueous phase on the other side. This is primarily determined by the molecule's desolvation cost — how much energy is required to strip away the hydration shell of polar groups before entering the hydrophobic membrane interior.

Molecular features favoring high PAMPA permeability: low polar surface area (TPSA < 80 Å² for high permeability, 80-120 Å² for moderate) is the single most predictive descriptor. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 2-3) — each donor adds roughly 10 Å² of TPSA and a strong water interaction that must be broken. Moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) provides the driving force for membrane partitioning. Molecular weight < 500 Da. Intramolecular hydrogen bonds can "mask" polar groups and improve permeability beyond what TPSA alone would predict — this is exploited in cyclic peptide drug design. Compact, low-flexibility conformations reduce the entropic cost of membrane insertion.

Features associated with poor PAMPA permeability: high TPSA (>120 Å²) is the dominant negative predictor. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 4) strongly reduce permeability. Charged species at the assay pH (typically pH 7.4) — carboxylates, phosphates, quaternary amines — have very poor passive diffusion because the charge cannot be buried in the lipid interior. Very hydrophilic molecules (logP < 0) lack the driving force for membrane partitioning. High molecular weight (>600 Da) and many rotatable bonds (>10) also reduce permeability.

Mutagenicity in the Ames test arises through several distinct mechanisms. Unlike Caco-2 cell assays, PAMPA has no active transporters, no efflux pumps, and no paracellular pathway — it isolates pure passive diffusion. The NCATS variant uses a standardized protocol across a large compound library.

The rate of passive diffusion is governed by the drug's ability to partition from aqueous solution into the lipid bilayer, diffuse across it, and re-partition into the aqueous phase on the other side. This is primarily determined by the molecule's desolvation cost — how much energy is required to strip away the hydration shell of polar groups before entering the hydrophobic membrane interior.

Molecular features favoring high PAMPA permeability: low polar surface area (TPSA < 80 Å² for high permeability, 80-120 Å² for moderate) is the single most predictive descriptor. Moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) provides the driving force for membrane partitioning. Molecular weight < 500 Da. Intramolecular hydrogen bonds can "mask" polar groups and improve permeability beyond what TPSA alone would predict — this is exploited in cyclic peptide drug design. Compact, low-flexibility conformations reduce the entropic cost of membrane insertion.

Features associated with poor PAMPA permeability: high TPSA (>120 Å²) is the dominant negative predictor. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 4) strongly reduce permeability. Charged species at the assay pH (typically pH 7.4) — carboxylates, phosphates, quaternary amines — have very poor passive diffusion because the charge cannot be buried in the lipid interior. Very hydrophilic molecules (logP < 0) lack the driving force for membrane partitioning. High molecular weight (>600 Da) and many rotatable bonds (>10) also reduce permeability.

Mutagenicity in the Ames test arises through several distinct mechanisms. Direct-acting mutagens are electrophilic species that react covalently with DNA bases — alkylating agents (epoxides, aziridines, nitrogen mustards, alkyl halides), Michael acceptors (α,β-unsaturated carbonyls, acrylates, vinyl sulfones), and acylating agents. Drug-induced hERG blockade prolongs the QT interval and can trigger fatal torsades de pointes arrhythmia. hERG is notoriously promiscuous — its inner cavity is unusually large and lipophilic compared to other potassium channels, making it a frequent off-target for diverse drug scaffolds.

The primary binding site is the inner cavity of the channel pore, accessible from the intracellular side when the channel is open. Two aromatic residues are critical: Tyr652 and Phe656 on the S6 helix, which line the cavity and form cation-π and π-stacking interactions with drug molecules. The cavity is roughly 10-12 Å in diameter and can accommodate molecules with extended conformations. Additional contacts involve Thr623, Ser624, and Val625 at the base of the selectivity filter. Unlike most K+ channels, hERG lacks the Pro-Val-Pro motif in S6, creating a wider, more drug-accessible cavity.

The dominant molecular recognition mechanism is cation-π interaction: a protonated (cationic) basic amine in the drug interacts with the aromatic π-systems of Tyr652 and Phe656. This is why a basic nitrogen with pKa well above physiological pH (so that it is predominantly protonated at pH 7.4) is the single most important feature of hERG blockers. Molecules with multiple aromatic rings can additionally engage in π-stacking with these residues, and lipophilic character promotes partitioning into the hydrophobic channel cavity.

Drug-induced hERG blockade prolongs the QT interval and can trigger fatal torsades de pointes arrhythmia. hERG is notoriously promiscuous — its inner cavity is unusually large and lipophilic compared to other potassium channels, making it a frequent off-target for diverse drug scaffolds.

The primary binding site is the inner cavity of the channel pore, accessible from the intracellular side when the channel is open. Two aromatic residues are critical: Tyr652 and Phe656 on the S6 helix, which line the cavity and form cation-π and π-stacking interactions with drug molecules. The cavity is roughly 10-12 Å in diameter and can accommodate molecules with extended conformations. Additional contacts involve Thr623, Ser624, and Val625 at the base of the selectivity filter. Unlike most K+ channels, hERG lacks the Pro-Val-Pro motif in S6, creating a wider, more drug-accessible cavity.

The dominant molecular recognition mechanism is cation-π interaction: a protonated (cationic) basic amine in the drug interacts with the aromatic π-systems of Tyr652 and Phe656. This is why a basic nitrogen with pKa well above physiological pH (so that it is predominantly protonated at pH 7.4) is the single most important feature of hERG blockers. Molecules with multiple aromatic rings can additionally engage in π-stacking with these residues, and lipophilic character promotes partitioning into the hydrophobic channel cavity.

The NCATS variant uses a standardized protocol across a large compound library.

The rate of passive diffusion is governed by the drug's ability to partition from aqueous solution into the lipid bilayer, diffuse across it, and re-partition into the aqueous phase on the other side. This is primarily determined by the molecule's desolvation cost — how much energy is required to strip away the hydration shell of polar groups before entering the hydrophobic membrane interior.

Charged species at the assay pH (typically pH 7.4) — carboxylates, phosphates, quaternary amines — have very poor passive diffusion because the charge cannot be buried in the lipid interior. Context: The Parallel Artificial Membrane Permeability Assay (PAMPA) measures passive transcellular permeability by quantifying how much compound diffuses across an artificial lipid membrane (typically a phospholipid mixture on a filter support) from a donor to an acceptor compartment. Unlike Caco-2 cell assays, PAMPA has no active transporters, no efflux pumps, and no paracellular pathway — it isolates pure passive diffusion. The NCATS variant uses a standardized protocol across a large compound library.

The rate of passive diffusion is governed by the drug's ability to partition from aqueous solution into the lipid bilayer, diffuse across it, and re-partition into the aqueous phase on the other side. This is primarily determined by the molecule's desolvation cost — how much energy is required to strip away the hydration shell of polar groups before entering the hydrophobic membrane interior.

Molecular features favoring high PAMPA permeability: low polar surface area (TPSA < 80 Å² for high permeability, 80-120 Å² for moderate) is the single most predictive descriptor. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 2-3) — each donor adds roughly 10 Å² of TPSA and a strong water interaction that must be broken. Moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) provides the driving force for membrane partitioning. Molecular weight < 500 Da. Intramolecular hydrogen bonds can "mask" polar groups and improve permeability beyond what TPSA alone would predict — this is exploited in cyclic peptide drug design. Compact, low-flexibility conformations reduce the entropic cost of membrane insertion.

Features associated with poor PAMPA permeability: high TPSA (>120 Å²) is the dominant negative predictor. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 4) strongly reduce permeability. Charged species at the assay pH (typically pH 7.4) — carboxylates, phosphates, quaternary amines — have very poor passive diffusion because the charge cannot be buried in the lipid interior. Very hydrophilic molecules (logP < 0) lack the driving force for membrane partitioning. High molecular weight (>600 Da) and many rotatable bonds (>10) also reduce permeability.

Context: The Parallel Artificial Membrane Permeability Assay (PAMPA) measures passive transcellular permeability by quantifying how much compound diffuses across an artificial lipid membrane (typically a phospholipid mixture on a filter support) from a donor to an acceptor compartment. Unlike Caco-2 cell assays, PAMPA has no active transporters, no efflux pumps, and no paracellular pathway — it isolates pure passive diffusion. The NCATS variant uses a standardized protocol across a large compound library.

The rate of passive diffusion is governed by the drug's ability to partition from aqueous solution into the lipid bilayer, diffuse across it, and re-partition into the aqueous phase on the other side. This is primarily determined by the molecule's desolvation cost — how much energy is required to strip away the hydration shell of polar groups before entering the hydrophobic membrane interior.

Molecular features favoring high PAMPA permeability: low polar surface area (TPSA < 80 Å² for high permeability, 80-120 Å² for moderate) is the single most predictive descriptor. Few hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 2-3) — each donor adds roughly 10 Å² of TPSA and a strong water interaction that must be broken. Moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) provides the driving force for membrane partitioning. Molecular weight < 500 Da. Intramolecular hydrogen bonds can "mask" polar groups and improve permeability beyond what TPSA alone would predict — this is exploited in cyclic peptide drug design. Compact, low-flexibility conformations reduce the entropic cost of membrane insertion.

Features associated with poor PAMPA permeability: high TPSA (>120 Å²) is the dominant negative predictor. Multiple hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≥ 4) strongly reduce permeability. Charged species at the assay pH (typically pH 7.4) — carboxylates, phosphates, quaternary amines — have very poor passive diffusion because the charge cannot be buried in the lipid interior. Very hydrophilic molecules (logP < 0) lack the driving force for membrane partitioning. High molecular weight (>600 Da) and many rotatable bonds (>10) also reduce permeability.

Charged species at the assay pH (typically pH 7.4) — carboxylates, phosphates, quaternary amines — have very poor passive diffusion because the charge cannot be buried in the lipid interior.
